case_info.scenario: An African American patient in their early 60s with a medical history significant for recent diagnosis of monoclonal gammopathy of unknown significance (MGUS) and prostate cancer was referred to the oculoplastic service for evaluation of intermittent, bilateral swelling and pain of their medial upper eyelids only for the past 2 years. They denied pruritus. Episodes occurred every few months and lasted for a few weeks at a time, with no obvious triggers. The patient denied other ocular symptoms and had no other skin findings. Their examination was notable for mild upper eyelid spongy edema with hyperpigmented, ecchymotic-appearing redundant skin overhanging the eyelid margins (Figure 1). There were no palpable nodules, and there was no lymphadenopathy. Review of systems was negative for fatigue, generalized muscle weakness, or neurologic deficits.

case_info.explanation: A. Biopsy the eyelid skin The differential diagnosis for noninfectious eyelid swelling includes autoimmune blepharochalasis, sarcoidosis, thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy, lupus erythematosus, dacryoadenitis, or idiopathic orbital inflammation. Other possible diagnoses include hereditary angioedema, atopic dermatitis, periocular rosacea, eczema, and localized cutis laxa. Given the lack of orbital signs such as proptosis or extraocular motility restriction, imaging is unnecessary (option B). Empirical topical corticosteroids (option C) may provide symptomatic relief but can mask an underlying etiology. Because this patient had no clinical signs of thyroid ophthalmopathy, serologies (option D) are unnecessary. Based on this patient’s history of MGUS, there was suspicion for an underlying systemic process and biopsy was undertaken (option A). The association of MGUS with cutaneous amyloidosis is exceedingly rare1; however, MGUS is a suspected precursor of multiple myeloma and light-chain amyloidosis, which are both associated with cutaneous disease.2,3Hematoxylin-eosin stain showed deposition of amorphous eosinophilic material in the dermis, which was positive for Congo red stain with birefringence, consistent with amyloid (Figure 2). Subsequent systemic workup by the hematology service was negative. Periocular amyloidosis is a rare disease characterized by extracellular deposition of proteinaceous insoluble fibrils in the conjunctiva, eyelid, or in the orbit.4When such deposition is unrelated to systemic disease, ie, primary localized cutaneous amyloidosis (PLCA), repeated friction, scratching, and sun exposure are thought to be causative.5Its clinical presentation varies widely, which may delay diagnosis by years. Typical findings are diffuse eyelid thickening, blepharoptosis, and recurrent subcutaneous or subconjunctival hemorrhages.4Deeper orbital disease can manifest with subjective pressure sensation, proptosis, and extraocular motility restriction.4Orbital imaging is not diagnostic but can be helpful in localizing the disease. Ultimately, tissue biopsy with pathognomonic red-green dichroism after Congo red staining and viewing in intense unidirectional polarized light is required.5 Once the diagnosis is confirmed, systemic workup for amyloidosis or plasma cell dyscrasia is required as 15% to 50% of patients have or will develop systemic disease.6Because amyloid deposition occurs in a cumulative, progressive fashion culminating in organ failure and death, early detection and intervention are key and may improve outcomes.3,6It is not known whether periocular amyloidosis has a higher or lower rate of systemic involvement. Given the relative rarity of this presentation, there is no treatment consensus. Cutaneous periocular disease is commonly observed, but en bloc resection, surgical debulking, and radiation have also been reported.4,7Unlike PLCA, where chronic itch-scratch cycle drives disease pathogenesis, periocular disease has not been associated with pruritus.4,7However, if pruritus is present, every effort should be made to control it with topical or systemic immunomodulators, as breaking the itch-scratch cycle can halt progression.8Unfortunately, pruritus is often refractory to medical therapies including corticosteroids, topical tacrolimus, phototherapy, laser therapy, oral retinoids, cyclosporine, cyclophosphamide, and thalidomide. Recently, there have been limited case reports suggesting a good response to Janus kinase inhibitors.8For deeper space-occupying lesions in the orbit, debulking may be considered.4Rates of recurrence after treatment may be as high as 21%.4 Although there are no reported data in the literature regarding racial predilection of cutaneous amyloidosis, many of its identifying clinical features are derived from experiences with White skin.2,4-7,9Behera et al10have previously shown in a South Asian population that certain “classic” dermoscopic features may not be present in dark-pigmented skin. This report of primary cutaneous amyloidosis in an African American patient adds to the small existing body of knowledge regarding this disease presentation in dark-pigmented skin.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: A. Biopsy the eyelid skin The differential diagnosis for noninfectious eyelid swelling includes autoimmune blepharochalasis, sarcoidosis, thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy, lupus erythematosus, dacryoadenitis, or idiopathic orbital inflammation. Other possible diagnoses include hereditary angioedema, atopic dermatitis, periocular rosacea, eczema, and localized cutis laxa. Given the lack of orbital signs such as proptosis or extraocular motility restriction, imaging is unnecessary (option B). Empirical topical corticosteroids (option C) may provide symptomatic relief but can mask an underlying etiology. Because this patient had no clinical signs of thyroid ophthalmopathy, serologies (option D) are unnecessary. Based on this patient’s history of MGUS, there was suspicion for an underlying systemic process and biopsy was undertaken (option A). The association of MGUS with cutaneous amyloidosis is exceedingly rare1; however, MGUS is a suspected precursor of multiple myeloma and light-chain amyloidosis, which are both associated with cutaneous disease.2,3Hematoxylin-eosin stain showed deposition of amorphous eosinophilic material in the dermis, which was positive for Congo red stain with birefringence, consistent with amyloid (Figure 2). Subsequent systemic workup by the hematology service was negative. Periocular amyloidosis is a rare disease characterized by extracellular deposition of proteinaceous insoluble fibrils in the conjunctiva, eyelid, or in the orbit.4When such deposition is unrelated to systemic disease, ie, primary localized cutaneous amyloidosis (PLCA), repeated friction, scratching, and sun exposure are thought to be causative.5Its clinical presentation varies widely, which may delay diagnosis by years. Typical findings are diffuse eyelid thickening, blepharoptosis, and recurrent subcutaneous or subconjunctival hemorrhages.4Deeper orbital disease can manifest with subjective pressure sensation, proptosis, and extraocular motility restriction.4Orbital imaging is not diagnostic but can be helpful in localizing the disease. Ultimately, tissue biopsy with pathognomonic red-green dichroism after Congo red staining and viewing in intense unidirectional polarized light is required.5 Once the diagnosis is confirmed, systemic workup for amyloidosis or plasma cell dyscrasia is required as 15% to 50% of patients have or will develop systemic disease.6Because amyloid deposition occurs in a cumulative, progressive fashion culminating in organ failure and death, early detection and intervention are key and may improve outcomes.3,6It is not known whether periocular amyloidosis has a higher or lower rate of systemic involvement. Given the relative rarity of this presentation, there is no treatment consensus. Cutaneous periocular disease is commonly observed, but en bloc resection, surgical debulking, and radiation have also been reported.4,7Unlike PLCA, where chronic itch-scratch cycle drives disease pathogenesis, periocular disease has not been associated with pruritus.4,7However, if pruritus is present, every effort should be made to control it with topical or systemic immunomodulators, as breaking the itch-scratch cycle can halt progression.8Unfortunately, pruritus is often refractory to medical therapies including corticosteroids, topical tacrolimus, phototherapy, laser therapy, oral retinoids, cyclosporine, cyclophosphamide, and thalidomide. Recently, there have been limited case reports suggesting a good response to Janus kinase inhibitors.8For deeper space-occupying lesions in the orbit, debulking may be considered.4Rates of recurrence after treatment may be as high as 21%.4 Although there are no reported data in the literature regarding racial predilection of cutaneous amyloidosis, many of its identifying clinical features are derived from experiences with White skin.2,4-7,9Behera et al10have previously shown in a South Asian population that certain “classic” dermoscopic features may not be present in dark-pigmented skin. This report of primary cutaneous amyloidosis in an African American patient adds to the small existing body of knowledge regarding this disease presentation in dark-pigmented skin.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: A. Biopsy the eyelid skin The differential diagnosis for noninfectious eyelid swelling includes autoimmune blepharochalasis, sarcoidosis, thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy, lupus erythematosus, dacryoadenitis, or idiopathic orbital inflammation. Other possible diagnoses include hereditary angioedema, atopic dermatitis, periocular rosacea, eczema, and localized cutis laxa. Given the lack of orbital signs such as proptosis or extraocular motility restriction, imaging is unnecessary (option B). Empirical topical corticosteroids (option C) may provide symptomatic relief but can mask an underlying etiology. Because this patient had no clinical signs of thyroid ophthalmopathy, serologies (option D) are unnecessary. Based on this patient’s history of MGUS, there was suspicion for an underlying systemic process and biopsy was undertaken (option A). The association of MGUS with cutaneous amyloidosis is exceedingly rare1; however, MGUS is a suspected precursor of multiple myeloma and light-chain amyloidosis, which are both associated with cutaneous disease.2,3Hematoxylin-eosin stain showed deposition of amorphous eosinophilic material in the dermis, which was positive for Congo red stain with birefringence, consistent with amyloid (Figure 2). Subsequent systemic workup by the hematology service was negative. Periocular amyloidosis is a rare disease characterized by extracellular deposition of proteinaceous insoluble fibrils in the conjunctiva, eyelid, or in the orbit.4When such deposition is unrelated to systemic disease, ie, primary localized cutaneous amyloidosis (PLCA), repeated friction, scratching, and sun exposure are thought to be causative.5Its clinical presentation varies widely, which may delay diagnosis by years. Typical findings are diffuse eyelid thickening, blepharoptosis, and recurrent subcutaneous or subconjunctival hemorrhages.4Deeper orbital disease can manifest with subjective pressure sensation, proptosis, and extraocular motility restriction.4Orbital imaging is not diagnostic but can be helpful in localizing the disease. Ultimately, tissue biopsy with pathognomonic red-green dichroism after Congo red staining and viewing in intense unidirectional polarized light is required.5 Once the diagnosis is confirmed, systemic workup for amyloidosis or plasma cell dyscrasia is required as 15% to 50% of patients have or will develop systemic disease.6Because amyloid deposition occurs in a cumulative, progressive fashion culminating in organ failure and death, early detection and intervention are key and may improve outcomes.3,6It is not known whether periocular amyloidosis has a higher or lower rate of systemic involvement. Given the relative rarity of this presentation, there is no treatment consensus. Cutaneous periocular disease is commonly observed, but en bloc resection, surgical debulking, and radiation have also been reported.4,7Unlike PLCA, where chronic itch-scratch cycle drives disease pathogenesis, periocular disease has not been associated with pruritus.4,7However, if pruritus is present, every effort should be made to control it with topical or systemic immunomodulators, as breaking the itch-scratch cycle can halt progression.8Unfortunately, pruritus is often refractory to medical therapies including corticosteroids, topical tacrolimus, phototherapy, laser therapy, oral retinoids, cyclosporine, cyclophosphamide, and thalidomide. Recently, there have been limited case reports suggesting a good response to Janus kinase inhibitors.8For deeper space-occupying lesions in the orbit, debulking may be considered.4Rates of recurrence after treatment may be as high as 21%.4 Although there are no reported data in the literature regarding racial predilection of cutaneous amyloidosis, many of its identifying clinical features are derived from experiences with White skin.2,4-7,9Behera et al10have previously shown in a South Asian population that certain “classic” dermoscopic features may not be present in dark-pigmented skin. This report of primary cutaneous amyloidosis in an African American patient adds to the small existing body of knowledge regarding this disease presentation in dark-pigmented skin.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

Other possible diagnoses include hereditary angioedema, atopic dermatitis, periocular rosacea, eczema, and localized cutis laxa. Given the lack of orbital signs such as proptosis or extraocular motility restriction, imaging is unnecessary (option B). Empirical topical corticosteroids (option C) may provide symptomatic relief but can mask an underlying etiology. Because this patient had no clinical signs of thyroid ophthalmopathy, serologies (option D) are unnecessary. Based on this patient’s history of MGUS, there was suspicion for an underlying systemic process and biopsy was undertaken (option A). The association of MGUS with cutaneous amyloidosis is exceedingly rare1; however, MGUS is a suspected precursor of multiple myeloma and light-chain amyloidosis, which are both associated with cutaneous disease.2,3Hematoxylin-eosin stain showed deposition of amorphous eosinophilic material in the dermis, which was positive for Congo red stain with birefringence, consistent with amyloid (Figure 2). Subsequent systemic workup by the hematology service was negative. Periocular amyloidosis is a rare disease characterized by extracellular deposition of proteinaceous insoluble fibrils in the conjunctiva, eyelid, or in the orbit.4When such deposition is unrelated to systemic disease, ie, primary localized cutaneous amyloidosis (PLCA), repeated friction, scratching, and sun exposure are thought to be causative.5Its clinical presentation varies widely, which may delay diagnosis by years. Typical findings are diffuse eyelid thickening, blepharoptosis, and recurrent subcutaneous or subconjunctival hemorrhages.4Deeper orbital disease can manifest with subjective pressure sensation, proptosis, and extraocular motility restriction.4Orbital imaging is not diagnostic but can be helpful in localizing the disease. Ultimately, tissue biopsy with pathognomonic red-green dichroism after Congo red staining and viewing in intense unidirectional polarized light is required.5 Once the diagnosis is confirmed, systemic workup for amyloidosis or plasma cell dyscrasia is required as 15% to 50% of patients have or will develop systemic disease.6Because amyloid deposition occurs in a cumulative, progressive fashion culminating in organ failure and death, early detection and intervention are key and may improve outcomes.3,6It is not known whether periocular amyloidosis has a higher or lower rate of systemic involvement. Given the relative rarity of this presentation, there is no treatment consensus. Cutaneous periocular disease is commonly observed, but en bloc resection, surgical debulking, and radiation have also been reported.4,7Unlike PLCA, where chronic itch-scratch cycle drives disease pathogenesis, periocular disease has not been associated with pruritus.4,7However, if pruritus is present, every effort should be made to control it with topical or systemic immunomodulators, as breaking the itch-scratch cycle can halt progression.8Unfortunately, pruritus is often refractory to medical therapies including corticosteroids, topical tacrolimus, phototherapy, laser therapy, oral retinoids, cyclosporine, cyclophosphamide, and thalidomide. Recently, there have been limited case reports suggesting a good response to Janus kinase inhibitors.8For deeper space-occupying lesions in the orbit, debulking may be considered.4Rates of recurrence after treatment may be as high as 21%.4 Although there are no reported data in the literature regarding racial predilection of cutaneous amyloidosis, many of its identifying clinical features are derived from experiences with White skin.2,4-7,9Behera et al10have previously shown in a South Asian population that certain “classic” dermoscopic features may not be present in dark-pigmented skin. This report of primary cutaneous amyloidosis in an African American patient adds to the small existing body of knowledge regarding this disease presentation in dark-pigmented skin.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"

  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

Biopsy the eyelid skin The differential diagnosis for noninfectious eyelid swelling includes autoimmune blepharochalasis, sarcoidosis, thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy, lupus erythematosus, dacryoadenitis, or idiopathic orbital inflammation. Other possible diagnoses include hereditary angioedema, atopic dermatitis, periocular rosacea, eczema, and localized cutis laxa. Given the lack of orbital signs such as proptosis or extraocular motility restriction, imaging is unnecessary (option B). Empirical topical corticosteroids (option C) may provide symptomatic relief but can mask an underlying etiology. Because this patient had no clinical signs of thyroid ophthalmopathy, serologies (option D) are unnecessary. Based on this patient’s history of MGUS, there was suspicion for an underlying systemic process and biopsy was undertaken (option A). The association of MGUS with cutaneous amyloidosis is exceedingly rare1; however, MGUS is a suspected precursor of multiple myeloma and light-chain amyloidosis, which are both associated with cutaneous disease.2,3Hematoxylin-eosin stain showed deposition of amorphous eosinophilic material in the dermis, which was positive for Congo red stain with birefringence, consistent with amyloid (Figure 2). Subsequent systemic workup by the hematology service was negative. Periocular amyloidosis is a rare disease characterized by extracellular deposition of proteinaceous insoluble fibrils in the conjunctiva, eyelid, or in the orbit.4When such deposition is unrelated to systemic disease, ie, primary localized cutaneous amyloidosis (PLCA), repeated friction, scratching, and sun exposure are thought to be causative.5Its clinical presentation varies widely, which may delay diagnosis by years. Typical findings are diffuse eyelid thickening, blepharoptosis, and recurrent subcutaneous or subconjunctival hemorrhages.4Deeper orbital disease can manifest with subjective pressure sensation, proptosis, and extraocular motility restriction.4Orbital imaging is not diagnostic but can be helpful in localizing the disease. Ultimately, tissue biopsy with pathognomonic red-green dichroism after Congo red staining and viewing in intense unidirectional polarized light is required.5 Once the diagnosis is confirmed, systemic workup for amyloidosis or plasma cell dyscrasia is required as 15% to 50% of patients have or will develop systemic disease.6Because amyloid deposition occurs in a cumulative, progressive fashion culminating in organ failure and death, early detection and intervention are key and may improve outcomes.3,6It is not known whether periocular amyloidosis has a higher or lower rate of systemic involvement. Given the relative rarity of this presentation, there is no treatment consensus. Cutaneous periocular disease is commonly observed, but en bloc resection, surgical debulking, and radiation have also been reported.4,7Unlike PLCA, where chronic itch-scratch cycle drives disease pathogenesis, periocular disease has not been associated with pruritus.4,7However, if pruritus is present, every effort should be made to control it with topical or systemic immunomodulators, as breaking the itch-scratch cycle can halt progression.8Unfortunately, pruritus is often refractory to medical therapies including corticosteroids, topical tacrolimus, phototherapy, laser therapy, oral retinoids, cyclosporine, cyclophosphamide, and thalidomide. Recently, there have been limited case reports suggesting a good response to Janus kinase inhibitors.8For deeper space-occupying lesions in the orbit, debulking may be considered.4Rates of recurrence after treatment may be as high as 21%.4 Although there are no reported data in the literature regarding racial predilection of cutaneous amyloidosis, many of its identifying clinical features are derived from experiences with White skin.2,4-7,9Behera et al10have previously shown in a South Asian population that certain “classic” dermoscopic features may not be present in dark-pigmented skin. This report of primary cutaneous amyloidosis in an African American patient adds to the small existing body of knowledge regarding this disease presentation in dark-pigmented skin.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: A. Biopsy the eyelid skin The differential diagnosis for noninfectious eyelid swelling includes autoimmune blepharochalasis, sarcoidosis, thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy, lupus erythematosus, dacryoadenitis, or idiopathic orbital inflammation. Other possible diagnoses include hereditary angioedema, atopic dermatitis, periocular rosacea, eczema, and localized cutis laxa. Given the lack of orbital signs such as proptosis or extraocular motility restriction, imaging is unnecessary (option B). Empirical topical corticosteroids (option C) may provide symptomatic relief but can mask an underlying etiology. Because this patient had no clinical signs of thyroid ophthalmopathy, serologies (option D) are unnecessary. Based on this patient’s history of MGUS, there was suspicion for an underlying systemic process and biopsy was undertaken (option A). The association of MGUS with cutaneous amyloidosis is exceedingly rare1; however, MGUS is a suspected precursor of multiple myeloma and light-chain amyloidosis, which are both associated with cutaneous disease.2,3Hematoxylin-eosin stain showed deposition of amorphous eosinophilic material in the dermis, which was positive for Congo red stain with birefringence, consistent with amyloid (Figure 2). Subsequent systemic workup by the hematology service was negative. Periocular amyloidosis is a rare disease characterized by extracellular deposition of proteinaceous insoluble fibrils in the conjunctiva, eyelid, or in the orbit.4When such deposition is unrelated to systemic disease, ie, primary localized cutaneous amyloidosis (PLCA), repeated friction, scratching, and sun exposure are thought to be causative.5Its clinical presentation varies widely, which may delay diagnosis by years. Typical findings are diffuse eyelid thickening, blepharoptosis, and recurrent subcutaneous or subconjunctival hemorrhages.4Deeper orbital disease can manifest with subjective pressure sensation, proptosis, and extraocular motility restriction.4Orbital imaging is not diagnostic but can be helpful in localizing the disease. Ultimately, tissue biopsy with pathognomonic red-green dichroism after Congo red staining and viewing in intense unidirectional polarized light is required.5 Once the diagnosis is confirmed, systemic workup for amyloidosis or plasma cell dyscrasia is required as 15% to 50% of patients have or will develop systemic disease.6Because amyloid deposition occurs in a cumulative, progressive fashion culminating in organ failure and death, early detection and intervention are key and may improve outcomes.3,6It is not known whether periocular amyloidosis has a higher or lower rate of systemic involvement. Given the relative rarity of this presentation, there is no treatment consensus. Cutaneous periocular disease is commonly observed, but en bloc resection, surgical debulking, and radiation have also been reported.4,7Unlike PLCA, where chronic itch-scratch cycle drives disease pathogenesis, periocular disease has not been associated with pruritus.4,7However, if pruritus is present, every effort should be made to control it with topical or systemic immunomodulators, as breaking the itch-scratch cycle can halt progression.8Unfortunately, pruritus is often refractory to medical therapies including corticosteroids, topical tacrolimus, phototherapy, laser therapy, oral retinoids, cyclosporine, cyclophosphamide, and thalidomide. Recently, there have been limited case reports suggesting a good response to Janus kinase inhibitors.8For deeper space-occupying lesions in the orbit, debulking may be considered.4Rates of recurrence after treatment may be as high as 21%.4 Although there are no reported data in the literature regarding racial predilection of cutaneous amyloidosis, many of its identifying clinical features are derived from experiences with White skin.2,4-7,9Behera et al10have previously shown in a South Asian population that certain “classic” dermoscopic features may not be present in dark-pigmented skin. This report of primary cutaneous amyloidosis in an African American patient adds to the small existing body of knowledge regarding this disease presentation in dark-pigmented skin.
